You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

power_id text
1 Applying the same logic to our power analysis, we assumed that load attenuates by 23% the suppression effect observed by Vicente-Conesa et al. (2023, Experiments 1-3), whose 238 participants performed the same task without any concurrent task,foot_1 equivalent to Δ𝑔 𝑧 = -0.20 in the meta-analysis. In the confirmatory model fitted to these data (see Confirmatory Model), the suppression coefficient was 𝛽 Suppression = 0.081. Thus, this attenuation corresponds to 𝛽 Group×Suppression = -0.019. For H2, we will use the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure (Lakens et al., 2018; Schuirmann, 1987) to determine whether the suppression effect under load is practically equivalent to zero. We set the equivalence bounds at ±19% of the suppression effect observed in these data, a value close to the precision of the meta-analytic estimate under higher load (±20% of the estimated effect). Thus, H2 will be supported only if the 96% confidence interval for the suppression effect in the load group falls entirely within these bounds. Figure 1B illustrates both tests.
2;3;4;5 Finally, we estimated the power of both confirmatory tests through simulations (DeBruine & Barr, 2021; Franco-Martínez et al., 2026; Kumle et al., 2021) based on the LMM fitted to these data. In each simulated data set, we generated both groups from this model, modifying only the suppression effect in the load group (a 23% attenuation for H1 and no suppression for H2). Each of the 500 data sets simulated per sample size was analysed with the preregistered confirmatory model and tests (a one-sided test for H1 and two one-sided tests for H2, each at 𝛼 = .02). With 140 participants per group, the power was 90% for H1 and 95% for H2 (Figure 1C), with false-positive rates close to the nominal 2% level (2.0% for H1, and 2.0% and 1.4% for H2 at the upper and lower equivalence bounds). We therefore established 140 participants per group as the minimum sample size. However, we plan to recruit 160 participants per group to accommodate potential exclusions, increasing power to 96% for H1 and 98% for H2.
6;7 We will recruit 160 participants in each group, continuing until at least 140 per group meet the inclusion criteria. Simulations of the confirmatory linear mixed model (LMM) gave 90% (N = 140 per group) and 96% (N = 160 per group) power to detect a 23% attenuation of the suppression effect.
8;9 As for H1. Simulations gave 95% (N = 140 per group) and 98% (N = 160 per group) power to support equivalence if suppression is absent under load.
10 All participants in the load group who complete the session, before exclusions. Simulations gave more than 99% power in a worst-case scenario (mean accuracy of 62.2%, N = 160).
11 As for H1. Simulations gave 92% power for a capture effect of 0.016 log units, about the size of the smallest effect of interest for H1 (N = 140 per group).
12 Two outcome-neutral criteria (Henderson & Chambers, 2022), listed as ON1 and ON2 in Table 1, will determine whether H1 and H2 can be interpreted as tests of the role of executive resources in distractor suppression. First, participants in the load group must actually perform the concurrent task. To that aim, we will fit a mixed-effects logistic regression to the accuracy of each count verification, with a fixed intercept and a by-participant random intercept, and test whether its intercept, which estimates the log-odds of a correct verification, is above 0 (i.e., accuracy above .5) with a one-sided Wald z test. This test will include all participants in the load group who complete the session, before the exclusions described above. To estimate the power of this test, we simulated the worst case for our sampling plan, in which 140 of the 160 participants we plan to recruit in the load group are just at the inclusion threshold (63.9%), and the other 20 respond at chance. This gives a mean accuracy of 62.2%. Across 1,000 simulated data sets, the test had more than 99% power (see also Table 1). If this criterion is not met, neither H1 nor H2 will be interpreted as a test of executive load.
13 Second, the singleton distractor must still capture attention in the load group. Otherwise, a smaller or absent suppression effect in this group could simply mean that there was little capture to suppress, that participants did not search as intended, or that the data were too noisy to reveal any effect of the distractor. To that aim, we will test whether the capture effect in the load group, estimated from the confirmatory model with marginaleffects, is significantly larger than zero, regardless of whether capture differs between groups. Previous studies found that capture remained large under WM load (Gao & Theeuwes, 2020; Vicente-Conesa et al., 2024), and in the data of Vicente-Conesa et al. ( 2023) capture was about twice as large as suppression. In simulations without suppression in the load group (the scenario of H2), this test had 92% power with 140 participants per group for a capture effect of 0.016 log units, about the size of the smallest effect of interest for H1 (10% of the capture effect in these data). If this criterion is not met, neither H1 nor H2 will be interpreted as evidence about suppression under load.
14;15 to identify the smallest effects that the time-course analysis of the suppression effect and the analysis of how the load manipulation modulates explicit knowledge (see Exploratory Analyses) can detect with 90% power with 140 participants per group (Figure1D-E). These analyses can detect an attenuation of 80% in the increase of suppression across blocks compared to the control group (𝛽 Group×Suppression×Time = -0.021), and an attenuation of 60% in awareness, as measured by the model reported below (𝛽 Group×Distance = 0.71), fitted to the 158 participants of Experiments 1 and 2 ofVicente-Conesa et al. (2023).3

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To check (3)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .5 Because each target has a 50% chance of containing the relevant orientation, the correct count will follow a binomial distribution (n = period length, p = .5).
p = .5 Specifically, we will use a one-sided binomial test against chance (p = .5, 𝛼 = .02).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 4 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 14 code files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 22 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 8 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server. 11 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

4 of 8 scripts ran to the end: 2 did not reproduce, and 2 did not finish within our time limit.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • meta_analysis.R: osf_download

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • analysis.R
  • run_all.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • _apa_title.qmd

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • functions.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.
  • load_data.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 11 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. The code reads files that are only inside franfrutos/rr_executive_vsl-v1.0.1.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as unzip("rr_executive_vsl-v1.0.1.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked. 2 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 11 scripts: 4 ran without error, 2 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 3 were run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

a script hit a could not find function "..." error; we added the library() calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
meta_analysis.R osf_download (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

setwd() in the code

2 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
functions.R 1 (non-literal)
load_data.R 1 (non-literal)

Calls that install packages in the code

28 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

library() calls added

2 scripts use functions from packages they do not load themselves. The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run them we added the library() calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after adding library() calls it should make itself.

File library() calls added
analysis.R library(purrr)
run_all.R library(purrr)

Run by another script

3 scripts are run by another script with source(), so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

In a popular version of this task, participants are asked to find a shape singleton target (e.g., a diamond among circles) while ignoring a salient colour singleton distractor (e.g., a red figure among green figures) that captures attention, making visual search harder.

Furthermore, participants are slower to find the target when it appears in the HPDL, suggesting they have learned to suppress attention towards the region of the display more likely to contain the distractor.

In these tests, participants are first asked to report whether they noticed any regularity in the singleton distractor location and then asked to indicate the specific location where they believe the distractor appeared most frequently.

This finding supports the conclusion that this form of attentional bias cannot be explained in terms of top-down control: If participants are unaware of the regularity driving their performance in the task, it is difficult to see how it could be represented in participants’ goals.

The independence between WM resources and statistical learning dovetails with recent evidence that statistical learning can improve when participants are distracted (e.g., when they are mind-wandering; Vékony et al., 2025) and is often stronger for participants with weaker executive function abilities (Pedraza et al., 2024), a pattern suggesting that disengaging top-down control may paradoxically enhance statistical learning (Janacsek & Németh, 2022; Smalle et al., 2022).

In the first experiment, participants had to retain a sequence of dots during the search task (two in the low-load condition vs. four in the high-load condition) and compare them to a probe sequence after the search task.

Importantly, in the second and third experiments, participants had to retain and operate with a sequence of three (low-load condition) or four (high-load condition) numbers, conceptually replicating the manipulation used by M. Chen et al. (2019).

In other words, participants were not required to continuously update task-relevant information while performing the visual search task.

The mean accuracy if 140 of 160 participants are at the inclusion threshold (see Data Pre-processing and Exclusions) and the remaining 20 perform the task at chance.

Participants are likely to differ not only in their overall speed, but also in how much the distractor captures their attention and in how much they learn to suppress it.
