Method Participants

Based on our power analysis (see Sample Size Rationale), we plan to recruit 320 participants and randomly assign them to the load and control groups (160 per group).

Participants will be psychology students from the Autonomous University of Madrid (UAM), who will take part online in exchange for course credits. Because the task will be conducted in Spanish, they must be native Spanish speakers. They must also have normal or corrected-to-normal vision, including normal colour vision, and be naive to the purpose of the experiment.

Participants who do not complete the session will be replaced. If exclusions (see Data Pre-processing and Exclusions) leave fewer than 140 participants in either group, we will continue recruiting for that group until it reaches 140 participants who meet all inclusion criteria.foot_0

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the UAM (Ref..

Sample Size Rationale

To determine the sample size, we first needed to establish how large an attenuation of the suppression effect our design should detect. This is not a trivial decision, given that previous studies have found little evidence that WM load affects distractor suppression. Rather than choosing an arbitrary effect size, we used the available evidence to establish a smallest effect size of interest (Lakens et al., 2018). Specifically, we conducted a Bayesian meta-analysis of the standardised suppression effects (𝑔 𝑧 ) of the five experiments that, to our knowledge, have compared learned distractor suppression under lower and higher WM load (Gao & Theeuwes, 2020, Experiments 1-2; Vicente-Conesa et al., 2024, Experiments 1-3). Details of the meta-analytic procedure are provided in the Appendix.

The results showed large suppression effects under both lower (𝑔 𝑧 = 0.89, 95% CrI [0.72, 1.07]) and higher WM load (𝑔 𝑧 = 0.94, 95% CrI [0.76, 1.13]), with virtually no difference between them (Δ𝑔 𝑧 = 0.05, 95% CrI [-0.20, 0.30]; Figure 1A) and indeed numerically more suppression under high load. Although the estimated effect of WM load was close to zero, its 95% credible interval (CrI) was still compatible with attenuations of up to approximately 23% of the suppression effect under lower load (Δ𝑔 𝑧 = -0.20). We therefore set our smallest effect size of interest at a 23% attenuation, the largest effect that previous studies could not rule out.

Applying the same logic to our power analysis, we assumed that load attenuates by 23% the suppression effect observed by Vicente-Conesa et al. (2023, Experiments 1-3), whose 238 participants performed the same task without any concurrent task,foot_1 equivalent to Δ𝑔 𝑧 = -0.20 in the meta-analysis. In the confirmatory model fitted to these data (see Confirmatory Model), the suppression coefficient was 𝛽 Suppression = 0.081. Thus, this attenuation corresponds to 𝛽 Group×Suppression = -0.019. For H2, we will use the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure (Lakens et al., 2018; Schuirmann, 1987) to determine whether the suppression effect under load is practically equivalent to zero. We set the equivalence bounds at ±19% of the suppression effect observed in these data, a value close to the precision of the meta-analytic estimate under higher load (±20% of the estimated effect). Thus, H2 will be supported only if the 96% confidence interval for the suppression effect in the load group falls entirely within these bounds. Figure 1B illustrates both tests.

Finally, we estimated the power of both confirmatory tests through simulations (DeBruine & Barr, 2021; Franco-Martínez et al., 2026; Kumle et al., 2021) based on the LMM fitted to these data. In each simulated data set, we generated both groups from this model, modifying only the suppression effect in the load group (a 23% attenuation for H1 and no suppression for H2). Each of the 500 data sets simulated per sample size was analysed with the preregistered confirmatory model and tests (a one-sided test for H1 and two one-sided tests for H2, each at 𝛼 = .02). With 140 participants per group, the power was 90% for H1 and 95% for H2 (Figure 1C), with false-positive rates close to the nominal 2% level (2.0% for H1, and 2.0% and 1.4% for H2 at the upper and lower equivalence bounds). We therefore established 140 participants per group as the minimum sample size. However, we plan to recruit 160 participants per group to accommodate potential exclusions, increasing power to 96% for H1 and 98% for H2.

Using the same logic, we also conducted sensitivity analyses (Lakens, 2022)

Procedure and Design

Except for the concurrent executive task in the load group and the 3-s response window in both groups, the procedure and design will match those of Vicente-Conesa et al. (2023). Because the study requires a large sample, both groups will complete the task online, consistent with prior work on learned distractor suppression (de Waard et al., 2022; Duncan et al., 2026; Gao & Theeuwes, 2022; Golan et al., 2024; Hanne et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2021; Ivanov et al., 2024; Ivanov & Theeuwes, 2021). The task will be run in jsPsych (de Leeuw et al., 2023) and hosted on JATOS (Lange et al., 2015), using a version programmed from the original MATLAB program of Vicente-Conesa et al. (2023), and it can be accessed at https://github.com/franfrutos/rr_executive_vsl/tree/main/Materials/jspsych_task. To control for differences in participants' distance from the screen, we will scale stimulus size to this distance using the virtual chinrest developed by Li et al. (2020), so that stimuli will have the visual angles used by Wang and Theeuwes (2018a, 2018b). Before the task, participants will adjust the size of an image on their screen to match a standard-sized card (e.g., a credit card or an identity card).

Then, they will perform a blind-spot measurement by covering their right eye and focusing their Note. (A) Meta-analysis of previous load manipulations. The distributions at the bottom show the posterior of the meta-analytical estimates, with their medians (points) and 66% (thick lines) and 95% credible intervals (thin lines). (B) Illustration of the confirmatory tests. Power for the confirmatory tests (C) and sensitivity analyses for the exploratory tests (D, E). Ribbon shows 95% CI. S = suppression effect (LPDL -HPDL) in the load condition or group indicated by the subscript; Δ = equivalence bound of H2.

left eye on a central placeholder while a red circle moves leftward, pressing the space bar when the circle disappears. This process will be repeated five times, and the average will be used to estimate their distance from the screen.

Figure 2A illustrates the sequence of a visual search trial. After a 500-ms fixation cross (1° × 1°), a search display with eight figures arranged in an imaginary circle with a radius of 4° will appear on the screen for 3 s or until response. The intertrial interval will be 500 ms. In all trials, a different-shaped target (a diamond among circles or a circle among diamonds) will be present. Circles will have a radius of 1°, and diamonds will subtend 2° × 2°. In some trials, all the figures will be displayed in the same colour. In other trials, a colour singleton distractor (red among green figures or vice versa) will be present. Each figure will contain a vertical or horizontal line (0.15° × 1°). The line orientation will be chosen randomly in each trial.

Participants will be asked to find the target as quickly as possible and discriminate the line orientation, pressing the left-arrow key for horizontal and the up-arrow key for vertical. Error feedback will be presented at the end of the trial after a mistake or a time-out.

Each block will include 120 trials. There will be three experimental conditions: (1) no distractor (ND), in which all the figures will be displayed in the same colour (40 trials, 33%); (2) HPDL, in which the singleton distractor will be presented in one particular location (52 trials, 43%); and (3) LPDL, in which the distractor will appear at random in any of the remaining locations (28 trials, 24%). Trials of each condition will be presented randomly within each block.

The HPDL will be randomly set for each participant and will remain the same throughout the task.

As illustrated in Figure 2A, in distractor-present trials, 65% of the time the distractor will appear at the HPDL, and only 5% at each other location.

Each participant will complete six blocks. After each block, a message on the screen will indicate that they may rest as needed. Throughout the experiment, participants in the load group will also perform a concurrent executive task. Each block will be divided into 12 periods: four periods of 8 trials, four periods of 10 trials, and four periods of 12 trials. The order of the periods will be randomised within each block. Figure 2B shows the sequence of a period. At the Note. (A) Trial sequence. Participants report the orientation of the line inside the target with the left (horizontal) or up (vertical) arrow key. Error feedback follows incorrect responses and time-outs. The map shows how often the colour singleton distractor appears at each location. (B) A period of the counting task (load group only). Participants count the targets with the line orientation shown at the start of the period (here, vertical). After 8, 10, or 12 trials, they press S (yes) or N (no) to report whether the number shown matches their count.

beginning of each period, an instruction screen will indicate whether participants must count targets containing a vertical line or a horizontal line. The relevant line orientation will be randomly selected for each period.

Participants will then perform the visual search task as usual while tracking the number of targets containing the relevant line orientation. Therefore, on each trial, participants will not only identify the target and respond to the orientation of the line it contains, but also determine whether to count that target and, when appropriate, update the current count maintained in WM. At the end of each period, a number will be presented, and participants will indicate whether it corresponds to the number of targets containing the relevant line orientation in the preceding period by pressing the S ('yes') or N ('no') key. The number will be correct in half of the periods of each length and incorrect in the other half. Because each target has a 50% chance of containing the relevant orientation, the correct count will follow a binomial distribution (n = period length, p = .5). Incorrect numbers will be drawn from the same distribution and redrawn if they match the correct count for that period. In other words, correct and incorrect numbers will follow almost the same distribution, so participants will need to keep count to tell them apart. After this response, a new period will begin with a new counting instruction.

After reading the instructions of each task, participants will answer brief multiple-choice questions about them, which will be shown again until all answers are correct. Then, they will complete three practice trials of the search task, as in Vicente-Conesa et al. (2023), followed in the load group by one practice period of the counting task (eight trials) with feedback on the verification. In all practice trials, all the figures will be presented in the same colour, so no singleton distractor will be presented before the first block.

Similar to Vicente-Conesa et al. (2023, Experiment 1), participants will complete an awareness test consisting of two questions. In the first, we will ask participants whether they think that the singleton distractor appeared more often in one particular location. They will respond on a 1 (definitely not) to 6 (definitely yes) Likert scale. Regardless of their response, in the second question they will also be required to indicate the location they think contained the distractor on more occasions. An array of eight circles containing numbers from 1 to 8 will be presented on the screen, and participants will indicate their selection by typing the number inside the location they select as the HPDL.

Statistical Analyses

All analyses will be conducted in R (version 4.3.1; R Core Team, 2023). We will fit linear mixed models (LMMs) with lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and test their fixed effects using Satterthwaite's approximation to the degrees of freedom, as implemented in lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). We will also fit the mixed-effects logistic regression of ON1 with lme4 and the awareness model with glmmTMB (Brooks et al., 2017). Unless noted otherwise, all preregistered tests will be one-sided in the predicted direction, with 𝛼 = .02.

Data Pre-processing and Exclusions

We will apply the same pre-processing to both groups, in the following order. First, we will exclude participants who do not complete the session or who have more than 25% errors or time-outs in the search task from all analyses. Second, we will remove the first 20 trials of the first block. Third, we will include only trials with a correct response in the RT analysis. Fourth, we will exclude RTs below 200 ms. Finally, we will exclude RTs more than 2.5 SDs from each participant's mean. In addition, we will exclude participants in the load group if their count-verification accuracy is not above chance, as this would suggest that they did not devote sufficient resources to the concurrent task. Specifically, we will use a one-sided binomial test against chance (p = .5, 𝛼 = .02). With 72 verifications (12 per block), participants will thus need at least 46 correct responses (63.9%) to be included.

Confirmatory Model

Both hypotheses concern the suppression effect, that is, how much faster participants respond when the distractor appears in the HPDL than when it appears in the LPDLs. To estimate this effect and its difference between groups, log-transformed RTs will be analysed using an LMM including predictors Condition (HPDL, LPDL, ND), Group (control, load), and their interaction.

Rather than an omnibus test of Condition with little theoretical interest, we will use two planned contrasts that correspond to the effects of interest (Schad et al., 2020). The first, suppression (LPDL -HPDL), measures how much less the distractor interferes with search when it appears in the HPDL. The second, capture (LPDL -ND), measures how much the distractor slows down search when it appears elsewhere. Group will be coded -0.5 (control) and 0.5 (load), so its interaction with suppression directly estimates how much the suppression effect differs between the load and control groups. The model's formula, as implemented in lme4, will be as follows:

Participants are likely to differ not only in their overall speed, but also in how much the distractor captures their attention and in how much they learn to suppress it. To account for these differences, the model will include random slopes for both contrasts across participants, as Barr et al. (2013) recommend. If this model does not converge or yields a singular fit, we will simplify it (Bates et al., 2018). Specifically, we will first remove the random slope for capture and then the random slope for suppression. This order keeps the individual differences in suppression, the effect of interest, in the model for as long as possible.

Hypothesis Tests

H1 will be tested with the Group × Suppression coefficient of the confirmatory model (𝛽 Group×Suppression ), which estimates the difference in the suppression effect between the load and the control group (load minus control). Because H1 predicts a smaller suppression effect in the load group, we will use a one-sided test for this directional prediction. Thus, H1 will be supported if this coefficient is significantly smaller than zero.

We will test H2 using the suppression effect in the load group, estimated from the same model. A non-significant suppression effect would not be enough to show that suppression is absent (e.g., Altman & Bland, 1995). Instead, we will test whether the effect is small enough to be considered practically equivalent to zero, using the TOST procedure as implemented in the marginaleffects package (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024). Specifically, H2 will be supported if the suppression effect in the load group is significantly larger than -Δ and significantly smaller than +Δ, that is, if its 96% CI falls entirely within ±Δ. As explained in the Sample Size Rationale, Δ corresponds to 19% of the suppression effect in previous control data (Δ = 0.0154). For both hypotheses, we will report the estimates and their 95% CIs in both log units and ms.

Viewed together, H1 and H2 distinguish three possible outcomes (see Table 1). If both are supported, the load abolishes suppression. If only H1 is supported, the load attenuates suppression without abolishing it. Finally, if neither is supported, we will interpret this outcome as support for previous accounts in which distractor-location learning is independent of executive resources.

Outcome-Neutral Criteria

Two outcome-neutral criteria (Henderson & Chambers, 2022), listed as ON1 and ON2 in Table 1, will determine whether H1 and H2 can be interpreted as tests of the role of executive resources in distractor suppression. First, participants in the load group must actually perform the concurrent task. To that aim, we will fit a mixed-effects logistic regression to the accuracy of each count verification, with a fixed intercept and a by-participant random intercept, and test whether its intercept, which estimates the log-odds of a correct verification, is above 0 (i.e., accuracy above .5) with a one-sided Wald z test. This test will include all participants in the load group who complete the session, before the exclusions described above. To estimate the power of this test, we simulated the worst case for our sampling plan, in which 140 of the 160 participants we plan to recruit in the load group are just at the inclusion threshold (63.9%), and the other 20 respond at chance. This gives a mean accuracy of 62.2%. Across 1,000 simulated data sets, the test had more than 99% power (see also Table 1). If this criterion is not met, neither H1 nor H2 will be interpreted as a test of executive load.

Second, the singleton distractor must still capture attention in the load group. Otherwise, a smaller or absent suppression effect in this group could simply mean that there was little capture to suppress, that participants did not search as intended, or that the data were too noisy to reveal any effect of the distractor. To that aim, we will test whether the capture effect in the load group, estimated from the confirmatory model with marginaleffects, is significantly larger than zero, regardless of whether capture differs between groups. Previous studies found that capture remained large under WM load (Gao & Theeuwes, 2020; Vicente-Conesa et al., 2024), and in the data of Vicente-Conesa et al. ( 2023) capture was about twice as large as suppression. In simulations without suppression in the load group (the scenario of H2), this test had 92% power with 140 participants per group for a capture effect of 0.016 log units, about the size of the smallest effect of interest for H1 (10% of the capture effect in these data). If this criterion is not met, neither H1 nor H2 will be interpreted as evidence about suppression under load.

Exploratory Analyses

Beyond the confirmatory tests, we will conduct three exploratory analyses. First, although we have no specific theoretical predictions about errors in the search task, we will analyse them using a logistic mixed-effects model with a similar structure to the confirmatory model. We will also use the same approach to select the random-effects structure.

Second, suppression can emerge early in the task (Duncan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2019), but it may continue to change over several hundred trials (e.g., Hanne et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2026). Thus, the concurrent task might retard the learning process underlying suppression even if the overall effect remains relatively intact. To assess whether the load slows down learning, we will examine how the suppression effect changes across blocks in each group. To that aim, we will add Time to the confirmatory model, along with all its interactions with Group and Condition.

Because learning curves in similar attentional tasks are often well described by a power function (Garre-Frutos et al., 2024 , 2025 , 2026), we will log-transform Time. The key effect will be the Group × Suppression × Time interaction, which estimates whether suppression increases more slowly across blocks in the load group. Because a slower increase would make this interaction negative, we will use a one-sided test and conclude that load slows learning if the interaction is significantly smaller than zero. Although this prediction is directional, we consider the analysis exploratory because we do not know what effect size would be reasonable. We will code Condition and Group as in the confirmatory model and select the random-effects structure using the same procedure.

Finally, because the claim that distractor suppression is automatic rests on its apparent independence from both awareness and cognitive resources, we will examine whether the load reduces not only learning to suppress the HPDL, but also explicit knowledge of this location. To that aim, we will analyse the location that participants select in the second awareness question. 4Following Franco-Martínez et al. (2025), the probability of selecting each location will be modelled as a function of its distance from the HPDL, as follows: where 𝑑 𝑙 is the circular distance between location l and the HPDL (from 0 to 4), and 𝜆 𝑖 is the awareness gradient of participant i.

A larger gradient means that choices are more concentrated around the HPDL, whereas a gradient of zero corresponds to random choices. Because each participant gives a single response, we cannot estimate individual gradients precisely. Instead, the model estimates the mean gradient for each group, assuming individual gradients are normally distributed around it.

In other words, the awareness model is a mixed-effects logistic regression of each participant's choice among the eight locations, with Distance as a predictor and a random slope of Distance across participants. Following Muff et al. (2020), we will fit this model with glmmTMB and include the Group × Distance interaction. If the load reduces explicit knowledge, distance from the HPDL should have a weaker influence on choices in the load group, making this interaction positive. As in the time-course analysis, we will use a one-sided test and conclude that the load reduces explicit knowledge if the interaction is significantly larger than zero.

Appendix Meta-Analysis of Previous Load Manipulations

To set the smallest effect size of interest for H1 and the equivalence bounds for H2 (see Sample Size Rationale), we meta-analysed the experiments that have compared learned distractor suppression under lower and higher WM load (Figure 1A). This appendix describes how we selected these experiments, computed their effect sizes, and combined them.

Studies

We included all experiments that, to our knowledge, measured suppression of a high-probability distractor location in the AST under two WM-load levels, manipulated across blocks or groups. We identified them in the review of Vicente-Conesa and Vadillo (2024) and in a search of OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar (October 2026). Five experiments met these criteria (Gao & Theeuwes, 2020, Experiments 1-2; Vicente-Conesa et al., 2024, Experiments 1-3), and Figure 1A shows their effects. We did not include four other studies. Two measured suppression of a distractor feature rather than a spatial location (J. Chen et al., 2026; Hamblin-Frohman & Becker, 2022). The other two did not manipulate load across blocks or groups. In Huang et al. (2025), participants held a location in memory in most search trials, which were intermixed with only a few trials without a memory task. In G. Zhao et al. (2024), load varied randomly from trial to trial, and participants searched in feature-search mode (Bacon & Egeth, 1994), which does not allow disentangling the effect of WM load on learning.

Effect Sizes

Because the experiments differed in overall response speed and in the variability of the suppression effect, we expressed the suppression effect under each load as a standardised effect size (Morris & DeShon, 2002), dividing it by the SD of participants' suppression scores pooled over the two loads, as follows: where 𝑀 LPDL -𝑀 HPDL is the mean suppression effect, 𝑆𝐷 pooled is the pooled SD of the suppression scores in between-participant designs and the root mean square of the two SDs in within-participant designs, and J is Hedges' small-sample correction (Hedges, 1981).

The sampling variance of each effect was as follows: where SD and n are the SD of the suppression scores and the number of participants under that load, and df are the degrees of freedom of 𝑆𝐷 pooled (n -1 in within-participant designs and 𝑛 1 + 𝑛 2 -2 in between-participant designs).

In within-participant designs, the two effects come from the same participants, so their sampling errors are correlated (Borenstein et al., 2009, Chapter 24). Their covariance is 𝑟 √ 𝑣 lower 𝑣 higher , where r is the correlation between participants' suppression effects under the two loads. Because Gao and Theeuwes (2020) tested each load in a separate session, we used the test-retest correlation of the suppression effect in the AST reported by Ivanov et al. (2024), r = .26, as an educated guess.

For Vicente-Conesa et al. (2024), we recomputed all statistics from their open data. For Gao and Theeuwes (2020), we read the mean suppression effects from their figures. In Experiment 1, we derived the SDs of participants' suppression scores from the reported t values (Lakens, 2013). In Experiment 2, however, they reported suppression effects only as significant (ps < .001). We therefore derived the SD of its suppression scores from the SDs of the HPDL and LPDL RTs, obtained from the error bars of their Figure 4 (SD = SE × √ 𝑛), and from the correlation between these RTs across participants (r):

This correlation was not reported, but it can be recovered from their Experiment 1, which used the same task, design, and sample size, by solving the same equation for r (r = .975, averaged across the two loads). This gave SDs of 64.9 ms without load and 55.9 ms with load. Because these SDs rest on values read from a figure and on a correlation taken from another experiment, we also conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding this experiment.

Meta-Analytic Model

We analysed the 10 effects with a Bayesian meta-regression in the brms package (Bürkner, 2017), which uses Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017). This model estimates the suppression effect under each load while accounting for the dependence between the two effects of each within-participant experiment. The model was as follows: where Load was coded -0.5 (lower load) and 0.5 (higher load), 𝑢 𝑖 ∼ Normal(0, 𝜏) captures the heterogeneity between effects, and the sampling errors 𝑒 𝑖 follow a multivariate normal distribution with the variances and covariances described above, which are treated as known (implemented with the fcor() term in brms).

Thus, 𝛽 0 estimates the mean suppression effect, and 𝛽 1 estimates its modulation by load. We used Normal(0, 1) priors for both coefficients, on the 𝑔 𝑧 scale, and a weakly informative half-Normal(0, 0.5) prior for 𝜏 (Röver et al., 2021). We ran four chains of 2,000 iterations (1,000 of warm-up), with a target acceptance rate of .95. All R values were below 1.01 (Vehtari et al., 2021), and there were no divergent transitions.

Results

The main results are reported in the Sample Size Rationale and Figure 1A. Heterogeneity between effects was low (𝜏 = 0.07, 95% CrI [0.00, 0.28]). In the sensitivity analysis excluding Gao and Theeuwes (2020, Experiment 2), both the largest attenuation and the half-width of the higher-load estimate were somewhat larger because fewer effects were pooled (28% and 22%, respectively). In other words, previous load manipulations left suppression practically intact, regardless of whether this experiment was included.

to identify the smallest effects that the time-course analysis of the suppression effect and the analysis of how the load manipulation modulates explicit knowledge (see Exploratory Analyses) can detect with 90% power with 140 participants per group (Figure1D-E). These analyses can detect an attenuation of 80% in the increase of suppression across blocks compared to the control group (𝛽 Group×Suppression×Time = -0.021), and an attenuation of 60% in awareness, as measured by the model reported below (𝛽 Group×Distance = 0.71), fitted to the 158 participants of Experiments 1 and 2 ofVicente-Conesa et al. (2023).3

Study Design

Specifically, we will invite as many new participants as are needed to reach 140 in that group. For example, if 135 participants in the load group meet the inclusion criteria, we will assign five more to this group, and we will repeat this step until 140 participants meet all criteria. Thus, each group will include between 140 and 160 participants.

The suppression effect in this data set (𝑔 𝑧 = 1.63, 95% CI [1.44, 1.83]) is similar to that of the seminal study of learned distractor suppression(Wang & Theeuwes, 2018a), which used the same number of trials per participant (𝑔 𝑧 = 1.94, 95%CI [1.27, 2.61]). This suggests that these data are representative of the effect typically observed with this task.

Experiment 1 used the same awareness test as the present study. In Experiment 2, participants ranked the three locations where they believed the distractor had appeared most often, so we treated the location ranked first as their choice(Franco-Martínez et al., 2025). We did not use Experiment 3, in which participants estimated how often the distractor had appeared at each location rather than selecting one.

If the load affects suppression and explicit knowledge differently, this would only qualify as a single dissociation(Stephens et al., 2019). Although informative, this pattern would not necessarily imply that the two measures reflect independent processes, since single-system models can also produce similar results(Berry et al., 2008; Kinder & Shanks, 2003).
